title: These lawyers got backed by Y Combinator without attending its program
excerpt: Y Combinator has backed many startups rethinking legal work for the ChatGPT-era. When two antitrust lawyers came along, it made them an unusual offer.
content_html:
2026-11-23T15:00:01.257Z

Y Combinator accepts just one in 100 applicants. That makes the famed startup accelerator nearly nine times as selective as Harvard Law School.

Jonathan Kanter and Doha Mekki, two former top Justice Department antitrust officials, didn't have to worry about those odds.

They got what Kanter calls the "VIP door."

Y Combinator agreed to lead the $6.4 million seed round for their new legal AI startup, FluxCap, writing a bigger check at a higher valuation than its standard deal, Kanter said. The founders also got the perks of the accelerator, including the network and credits for tech services, without attending the program in person.

The special treatment comes as Y Combinator has been pouring money into startups promising to reinvent legal work with artificial intelligence. One recent batch included not one, but four AI-native law firms.

FluxCap is making a different bet.

Kanter and Mekki, who spent the Biden years taking on corporate giants at the Justice Department, are building software for high-stakes legal cases, starting with antitrust. They say the platform helps lawyers sift through evidence, research the law, and build stronger cases.

The promise is that smaller teams can take on complex cases without needing an army of associates, Kanter and Mekki said.

Y Combinator runs its program in San Francisco four times a year, and each batch usually includes a handful of remote founders. FluxCap was affiliated with the spring 2026 cohort.

Luther Lowe, Y Combinator's head of public policy, declined to comment on the terms of FluxCap's deal. Instead, he pointed to the team's unusual mix of expertise.

"FluxCap pairs lawyers who have tried high-stakes cases with engineers who can build that judgment into the product," Lowe said in an email. "As legal tech moves into complex litigation, where mistakes are expensive, that combination is hard to replicate.'"

The BLT is overrated

Large language models made it easier than ever to build legal technology. A wave of startups followed, promising to free lawyers from the drudgery of document review and drafting so they could focus on more valuable work.

Kanter and Mekki argue too many of them started in the wrong place.

Instead of starting with what lawyers do, FluxCap's founders started with how lawyers think.

They set out to teach their system how an expert lawyer spots issues, connects facts to the law, and figures out which arguments are most persuasive. For more than a year, former Justice Department lawyers worked shoulder to shoulder with engineers from Palantir and Meta, testing the technology, picking apart its answers, and tweaking it.

Kanter calls this approach "deep legal tech." He has a less flattering name for software that automates legal tasks without truly understanding the law: BLTs. Basic legal tech.

He likens the challenge to building a self-driving car.

Waymo has the technology to drive without a person behind the wheel, he said, but that doesn't mean its cars can traverse any city straight out of the gate. They first need to understand the streets, intersections, and quirks of the places they're driving.

"Law's the same way," he said.

For FluxCap, that means mastering one area of law at a time. It's starting with antitrust, but Kanter and Mekki said the same underlying technology could eventually help lawyers with everything from regulatory advice to internal investigations.

Startups like Syllo and Everlaw also serve litigators specifically.

Boutique firms including Kressin Powers and Glenn Agre have rolled out FluxCap's tools. The company says it has also had talks with two state attorneys general's offices and a large city government.

But Kanter and Mekki think the bigger opportunity lies with law firms that don't exist yet. They expect more elite lawyers to leave Big Law and strike out on their own, using technology to take on meaty cases with smaller teams.

The ambition isn't just to build better software for lawyers, they said. It's to change how many lawyers it takes to build a formidable law firm.
